paragraphs: Swamiji explained that Rama is seen as the symbol of the Absolute, and Sita as the symbol of Power. Without time to tell her whole life, he chose one scene that he felt spoke especially to women.

During their years of exile, Sita and Rama went into the forest to visit a woman sage, her body worn thin by fasting and devotion. Sita bowed before her, and the sage laid a hand on her head and blessed her.

The sage counted Sita's blessings. A beautiful body is a great gift, and Sita had it. A noble husband is a greater gift, and Sita had that too. Greatest of all, said the sage, was to be perfectly obedient to such a husband, and Sita was that as well. Surely she must be happy.

Sita answered with quiet wisdom. She was grateful for her beauty and for so devoted a husband. But about the third blessing, she honestly could not say whether she obeyed him or he obeyed her. She remembered only this: when he took her hand before the sacred fire at their wedding, she felt, whether it was the fire's glow or God's own doing, that she was his and he was hers. Ever since, each had completed the other's life.
Swamiji noted that parts of this poem had been translated into English. In India, he said, Sita is the ideal of womanhood and is worshipped as God in human form.
learn: Sita's answer moves the idea of a good relationship from obedience to partnership. The strongest bonds, in friendship or marriage, are those where two people complete each other and neither keeps score of who gives way.
